deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page asks when x^3+y^3 is a square with x,y coprime. Euler sets p=x+y and q=x-y, so that x^3+y^3 = p(p^2+3q^2)/4, and splits by whether 3 divides p. Case I, where the two factors are coprime, ended on the previous page.

CASE II (3 | p). Put p=3r. Then p(p^2+3q^2) = 9 r(3r^2+q^2), so r(3r^2+q^2) must be a square.
(a) Take q=f^2-3g^2 and r=2fg. Then 3r^2+q^2 = (f^2+3g^2)^2. For r to be a square take f=2h^2 and g=k^2. This gives r=4h^2k^2, p=12h^2k^2 and q=4h^4-3k^4. [Mine: hence x=(4h^4+12h^2k^2-3k^4)/2, y=(12h^2k^2+3k^4-4h^4)/2, and x^3+y^3 = (3hk(4h^4+3k^4))^2.]
(b) Alternatively take q=(3g^2-f^2)/2 and r=fg. Then 3r^2+q^2 = ((f^2+3g^2)/2)^2. Put f=h^2 and g=k^2, so r=h^2k^2, p=3h^2k^2 and q=(3k^4-h^4)/2. Hence x=(p+q)/2=(3k^4+6h^2k^2-h^4)/4 and y=(p-q)/2=(h^4+6h^2k^2-3k^4)/4. With h=k=1: q=r=1, p=3, x=2, y=1, giving 8+1=9, the known case that the cube-root method of the previous page missed. [Mine: x^3+y^3 = (3hk(h^4+3k^4)/4)^2.]

FLT n=3 VIA x^4-4xz^3. If a^3+b^3=c^3, then c^6-4a^3b^3 = (a^3-b^3)^2. With x=c^2 and z=ab this says x(x^3-4z^3) = x^4-4xz^3 is a square (the 'supra observavimus').
- Euler assumes the factors are coprime, so each must be a square.
- To make x^3-4z^3 a square he uses the previous page's 'Aliter' parametrization with n=-4: x+z*4^(1/3)... more precisely x=a(a^3-8nb^3)=a(a^3+32b^3), z=4b(a^3+nb^3)=4b(a^3-4b^3). [Check: x^3-4z^3=(a^6-80a^3b^3-128b^6)^2.]
- Then x must be a square, so a(a^3+32b^3) must be a square. Writing c=-2b gives a^3+32b^3 = a^3-4c^3, so a(a^3-4c^3) is a square: the same form in (allegedly) smaller numbers.
- Iterating gives an infinite descent, impossible. The terminal case e=0 can only arise if z=0 from the start.

PROBLEM: make x^3+ny^3 a cube. Let θ = n^(1/3) and set x+yθ = (p+qθ+rθ^2)^3. Then the cube root of x^3+ny^3 is the norm p^3+nq^3+n^2r^3-3npqr. Expanding:
- x = p^3+6npqr+nq^3+n^2r^3,
- y = 3p^2q+3npr^2+3nq^2r,
- 0 = 3p^2r+3pq^2+3nqr^2.
The last is a quadratic in p, giving p = (-q^2 ± sqrt(q^4-4nqr^3))/(2r). So q(q^3-4nr^3) must be a square, and (assuming coprime factors) each factor must be one.
- q=s^2, so s^6-4nr^3=t^2, i.e. (s^3+t)(s^3-t)=4n r^3. [Implicit: r=fg.]
- Choosing s^3+t=2f^3 and s^3-t=2ng^3 gives s^3 = f^3+ng^3, the same equation in smaller numbers.
- Euler concludes: if no solution exists in small numbers, none exists in large ones (a conditional descent).

The page ends with the start of Lexell's fragment. For FLT a^λ+b^λ=c^λ it uses c^{2λ}-4a^λb^λ=(a^λ-b^λ)^2, continued on the next page.
errors: Repeated unjustified coprimality assumptions. From x(x^3-4z^3)=□, from a(a^3+32b^3)=□ and from q(q^3-4nr^3)=□, Euler concludes each factor is a square without controlling common divisors (e.g. powers of 2 and divisors of n).

The parametrization of x^3-4z^3=□ (and of x+y·n^(1/3) as an exact square or cube) is assumed to give all solutions. This needs unique factorization in Z[n^(1/3)] and ignores units. The real cubic field Q(n^(1/3)) has a unit of infinite order, so x+yθ need only be a unit times a square or cube. This is a serious gap.
The claim that the new numbers a, c (resp. f, g) are 'manifestly much smaller' is asserted, not proved.

In the cube problem, the split s^3+t=2f^3, s^3-t=2ng^3 is only one of several possible distributions of the factors of 4n f^3 g^3. The conclusion is only conditional, and indeed x^3+ny^3 = cube does have nontrivial solutions for many n (e.g. n=7: 1+7=8).
Slip in the original: 'quam illi x et y' should read 'x et z' (the variables of x(x^3-4z^3)).

results.what: Parametric solutions of x^3+y^3=square in the case 3|(x+y): x=(3k^4+6h^2k^2-h^4)/4, y=(h^4+6h^2k^2-3k^4)/4 (and a companion family), recovering 1^3+2^3=3^2
results.modern_name: rational points / parametrizations on the curve x^3+y^3=z^2
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Algebra II and related papers); the problem goes back to Diophantus/Fermat-era work

results.what: Equivalence: a^3+b^3=c^3 implies x^4-4xz^3=□ (x=c^2, z=ab), with an attempted infinite descent on x(x^3-4z^3)=□
results.modern_name: descent on an elliptic curve (quartic model of the Fermat cubic, e.g. y^2=x^4-4x)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (FLT n=3, Algebra 1770, with a known gap); the descent framework goes back to Fermat

results.what: Using x+y·n^(1/3)=(p+qn^(1/3)+rn^(2/3))^k with the norm form p^3+nq^3+n^2r^3-3npqr to make x^3+ny^3 a square or cube
results.modern_name: factorization in the pure cubic ring Z[n^(1/3)] / norm-form method
results.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange (Lagrange's 1768-70 work on norm forms)

results.what: Descent for x^3+ny^3=cube via the discriminant q(q^3-4nr^3)=□, leading to s^3=f^3+ng^3
results.modern_name: descent via 3-isogeny on x^3+ny^3=z^3 (curve y^2=x^3-432n^2 type)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Algebra II, cube case); systematized much later (Sylvester, Selmer)

deep.surprise_reason: This page was published in the 1862 Opera Postuma and the descent ideas parallel Euler's known FLT n=3 work and Algebra. The use of cube-root irrationalities and the x^4-4xz^3 reformulation are interesting but known to belong to Euler's circle (Euler/Lexell). The arguments contain the familiar gaps.

checkable.asserts: the alternative parametrization q=(3g^2-f^2)/2, r=fg works
the final x,y of case II(b) make x^3+y^3 a square
the first family (f=2h^2, g=k^2) also makes x^3+y^3 a square
c^6-4a^3b^3=(a^3-b^3)^2 when c^3=a^3+b^3, so x(x^3-4z^3) is a square with x=c^2, z=ab
x=a(a^3+32b^3), z=4b(a^3-4b^3) makes x^3-4z^3 a square
the norm of p+qθ+rθ^2 is p^3+nq^3+n^2r^3-3npqr
the discriminant of the condition 0=p^2r+pq^2+nqr^2 is q(q^3-4nr^3)
s^3+t=2f^3, s^3-t=2ng^3 gives s^6-t^2=4n(fg)^3 and s^3=f^3+ng^3

In the descent paragraph the original reads 'quam illi x et y'; logically it should be x and z (a slip in the source, not in the transcription).
The expansion is laid out in the image as three columns: rational part, coefficient of n^(1/3), coefficient of n^(2/3). The linearized transcription is correct.
